page: Microsoft Azure M8ms is a memory-intensive server instance built on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features an Intel Xeon 8280M processor utilizing the x86_64 architecture, configured with 8 vCPUs across 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The CPU operates at a base speed of 2.7 GHz and includes a 105 MB L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 219.0 GB of system memory, yielding 27.34 GB of RAM per physical core. Local storage consists of a 262 GB volume, and the instance is Premium Storage capable. No GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses are included.

Benchmark results indicate a clear tradeoff between massive memory capacity and processing throughput. The instance demonstrates poor single-core CPU performance, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1036.79 and a Geekbench single-core score of 857.0, both falling into the bottom 10% of tested hardware. Multi-core performance is also limited, with a PassMark CPU score of 6389.48 and a stress-ng multi-core score of 5448.42, placing it in the bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth tests show a read-only large block speed of 36.63 GB/sec, though large block write performance achieves an average tier at 31.88 GB/sec.

Given the high memory-to-vCPU ratio of over 27 GB per vCPU, the M8ms is designed for memory-bound workloads rather than compute-heavy operations. PassMark database operations and Redis SET operations fall into the bottom 25%, indicating that while the instance can hold large datasets in memory, transaction processing speeds are constrained by the CPU. It is configured for large in-memory databases, caching layers, and enterprise applications requiring substantial memory footprints where raw CPU execution speed is not the primary bottleneck. Qualitatively, the instance offers high memory density per resource unit, making it cost-efficient specifically for memory-allocated licensing.

Benchmarks reveal a significant tradeoff: while memory capacity is exceptionally high, compute performance is constrained. Consequently, this instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound workloads rather than compute-intensive tasks. It is configured for large in-memory databases, caching layers, and enterprise applications that require massive memory footprints but have moderate processing demands.
